title: Sum of Reciprocal Odd Squares: $\sum 1/(2k+1)^2 = \pi^2/8$
description: Restricting the Basel sum ∑1/n² = π²/6 to the odd integers gives ∑_{k=0}^∞ 1/(2k+1)² = π²/8. Proved as an elementary corollary of Mathlib's hasSum_zeta_two by splitting the series into even- and odd-indexed subsequences (HasSum.even_add_odd): the even part rescales to π²/24, so by uniqueness of sums the odd tail is π²/6 − π²/24 = π²/8. Fully verified, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The **Basel problem** asks for the closed form of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty 1/n^2$, solved by **Euler** in 1734 with the value $\pi^2/6$. A standard companion question restricts the sum to the odd integers. Because $1/n^2$ is summable and absolutely convergent, the full sum splits cleanly into its even- and odd-indexed parts. The even-indexed terms $1/(2k)^2 = (1/4)\cdot 1/k^2$ reproduce the Basel series scaled by $1/4$, contributing $\pi^2/24$; the remaining odd part is therefore $\pi^2/6 - \pi^2/24 = \pi^2/8$. This identity is the $s=2$ case of the relation between the Riemann zeta function and the Dirichlet lambda function $\lambda(s) = (1 - 2^{-s})\zeta(s)$, here $\lambda(2) = (3/4)\zeta(2) = \pi^2/8$.
overview.problemStatement: OQ-06-01: Restrict the Basel identity to the odd integers — prove $\sum_{k=0}^\infty 1/(2k+1)^2 = \pi^2/8$ in Lean 4.
overview.text: Restricting the Basel sum ∑1/n² = π²/6 to the odd integers gives ∑_{k=0}^∞ 1/(2k+1)² = π²/8, proved as an elementary corollary of Mathlib's hasSum_zeta_two via the even/odd decomposition of the series.
overview.proofStrategy:
1. **Basel identity** (Mathlib): HasSum (fun n => 1/n²) (π²/6) via hasSum_zeta_two.
2. **Even part** (proved): the even-indexed subsequence k ↦ 1/(2k)² equals the Basel series scaled by 1/4, so HasSum (fun k => 1/(2k)²) (π²/24).
3. **Odd part summable** (proved): the odd-indexed subsequence is a reindexed subseries of a summable series (comp_injective).
4. **Combine** (proved): HasSum.even_add_odd reconstructs the full series from even + odd; uniqueness against the Basel value pins the odd sum to π²/8.
5. **Restate** (proved): in the natural (2k+1 : ℝ) form and as a tsum equality.
keyInsights: The result follows entirely from Mathlib's hasSum_zeta_two with no new analysis — the content is the even/odd decomposition plus the arithmetic identity π²/6 − π²/24 = π²/8.
HasSum.even_add_odd is the precise Mathlib tool: it splits a HasSum over ℕ into even- and odd-indexed subsequences, which is exactly the parity decomposition this proof needs.
The even part is handled by rescaling: 1/(2k)² = (1/4)·1/k², so HasSum.mul_left turns the Basel series into the even-square series (value π²/24).
Pinning the odd value uses uniqueness of sums (HasSum.unique) rather than computing the odd series directly — the unknown odd value b is determined by π²/6 = π²/24 + b.
This is the λ(2) = (3/4)ζ(2) special value of the Dirichlet lambda function; the companion even identity ∑1/(2k)² = π²/24 is recorded alongside.
prerequisites: Infinite series and HasSum / Summable in Mathlib
Even/odd subsequence decomposition of series over ℕ

sections.title: Setup: Sum of Reciprocal Odd Squares via Even/Odd Splitting
sections.summary: Derives ∑_{k=0}^∞ 1/(2k+1)² = π²/8 as an elementary corollary of the Basel identity, splitting ∑ 1/n² into even + odd subsequences via HasSum.even_add_odd. The even part rescales to (1/4)(π²/6) = π²/24, so by uniqueness of infinite sums the odd part is π²/6 − π²/24 = π²/8; also records the companion even-square identity ∑ 1/(2k)² = π²/24. 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
sections.mathContext: $\sum_n 1/n^2=\sum_k 1/(2k)^2+\sum_k 1/(2k+1)^2$ via `HasSum.even_add_odd`; the even part rescales to $\pi^2/24$, so uniqueness of sums gives the odd part $\pi^2/6-\pi^2/24=\pi^2/8$.

conclusion.summary: The odd-restricted Basel sum ∑1/(2k+1)² = π²/8 is fully formalized in Lean 4 with 0 sorries and 0 axioms, as an elementary corollary of Mathlib's hasSum_zeta_two via the even/odd decomposition of the series. The companion even identity ∑1/(2k)² = π²/24 falls out of the same argument.
conclusion.implications: Confirms that parity-restricted zeta values at s=2 are immediately accessible from the Basel identity in Mathlib. The same even/odd decomposition extends to higher even powers (e.g. ∑1/(2k+1)⁴ = π⁴/96) and to the Dirichlet lambda function λ(s) = (1−2^{-s})ζ(s).
